doc.title: Milt Hinton interviewed by Joe Williams, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

title: Joining Calloway: first Pullman, $100 a week and Ben Webster
summary: Hinton leaves Chicago with a bag of clothes and fried chicken, learns the pay is $100 a week, and meets Ben Webster, who became a dearest friend.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: a little canvas bag with a clean suit and underwear and I had to have a gabardine [inaudible] suit,” and I had to go to the South Street Station, and got on that bandstand.
She didn’t give you a little brown bag to take too?
Yeah well she had a little fried chicken.
A little fried chicken in there.
And I got on at the South Street Station. I’d never been on a Pullman in my life, Joe. You know I didn’t come from Mississippi on no Pullman.

I got on this Pullman, and there was all these great musicians on there, Doc Cheatham, Keg Johnson, Foots Thomas and all these guys. And I said Keg Johnson got me the gig, he recommended me, and I said to Keg, I say, “Keg, I didn’t ask Cab about no money or nothing,” I say, “He just told me to be here at nine o’clock.” He say, “Everybody in this band makes $100 a week.” I almost fainted. I almost fainted. I said I’ll be a millionaire in two months.
Well, and sure enough you are.

And listen to this. Ben Webster got on late. And I must have weighed about 109 pounds soaking wet. And Ben Webster staggered to the men’s room and me standing there being introduced to the band, and he said, “Now who is that?” He said, “What is that” talking about me. And Cab say, “That’s the new bass player.” He said, “A new what?” And I said I’d never like him as long as I lived. He turned out to be my dearest friend.
Yeah, he was fun guy. He was always putting people on, making people think he was a cad, but he wasn’t, he was really a good guy.
I learned so much from this man.
